article.title: Why Retention Rates Need a Clear Starting Population
article.why: Practical analytical English for data-driven decisions.

paragraphs.en: Retention rate sounds simple: count customers who remain active and divide by a customer base. The difficult part is defining that starting base. Different denominators can produce very different conclusions. Suppose 100,000 customers purchased last year and 70,000 of them purchase again this year. A basic annual retention rate is 70 percent. But what if 10,000 of the original customers became ineligible because they closed an account, moved outside the service area, or lost consent for the measured channel? Excluding them changes the denominator and the interpretation. Neither choice is automatically correct; it depends on the business question. If management wants to understand relationship persistence among everyone active last year, the original base is relevant. If a campaign team wants to evaluate customers who could actually receive treatment, an eligible base may be more useful. The definition of “active” also matters. One purchase, a minimum spending amount, or activity in a particular product can create different cohorts. Observation windows must be symmetric. Comparing twelve months of starting activity with only six months of follow-up will understate retention. New customers require special handling because they have shorter exposure. Cohort retention by acquisition month can make comparisons fairer. Reactivated customers should also be separated when the business wants to distinguish continuous relationships from win-back behavior. Data availability can create artificial churn. Identity changes, card replacements, source-system migration, or broken joins can make a continuing customer look lost. Reconciliation checks are therefore part of retention analysis. Segment rates need their own denominators. A 90 percent retention rate in a tiny premium tier may contribute fewer retained customers than a 60 percent rate in a large mass segment. Report both rates and counts. Revenue retention is another useful view. A company can retain many customers but lose substantial revenue if the customers who leave are disproportionately valuable. Conversely, customer retention can fall while revenue retention remains high. The best reporting states the cohort definition, eligibility rule, activity rule, follow-up window, and treatment of reactivation. Retention is not one universal number. It is a conditional probability defined on a specific starting population, and that population must be visible before the percentage can be trusted.  Analysts should document the population, observation window, assumptions, and operational definition. This makes the conclusion reproducible and helps separate a headline result from the mechanism that produced it.
